core: Working definition, attributed: fat-soluble vitamins are vitamins that dissolve in fat and are stored in the body's fat tissue (MedlinePlus: stored in liver, fatty tissue, and muscles)
The four fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, and K, each with one main job and original food examples
How they travel: absorbed with dietary fat, stated simply (absorption mechanics belong to the sibling absorption topic)
Storage: the body stores them in the liver, fatty tissue, and muscles; implication stated simply (no dosing)
Deficiency and excess: both are possible; toxicity is a real concern with very large supplement doses (factual only, NO supplementation advice)
Food sources: liver, dairy, eggs, leafy greens, vegetable oils, and sunlight for vitamin D — each named factually
Honest framing: fat-soluble vitamins are the pantry, not the fridge
supporting: Each vitamin's classic deficiency condition (night blindness/xerophthalmia for A; rickets and osteomalacia for D; bruising and slow clotting for K; rare nerve/muscle damage for E)
The skin limits vitamin D production from sunlight, so sun cannot cause toxic excess; high levels are almost always caused by supplements
Preformed vitamin A versus provitamin A carotenoids (beta-carotene) and their different toxicity profiles
Water-soluble contrast (C and the B vitamins, not stored) to sharpen the storage distinction
outOfScope: Vitamins as a class (own topic: nutrition:foundations:vitamins)
Supplements and supplementation advice (own topic: nutrition:foundations:supplements)
Digestion and absorption mechanics (own topic: nutrition:foundations:absorption)
Recommended amounts, upper limits, and dosing (general-literacy lesson names facts, not doses)

claims.claim: Fat-soluble vitamins are vitamins that dissolve in fat and are stored in the body's fat tissue; MedlinePlus states the fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the body's liver, fatty tissue, and muscles, and names exactly four: vitamins A, D, E, and K.

Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin important for normal vision, the immune system, reproduction, and growth; preformed vitamin A is found in fish, organ meats such as liver, dairy products, and eggs, while provitamin A carotenoids such as beta-carotene in plant foods are converted into vitamin A by the body.
The most common sign of vitamin A deficiency is xerophthalmia, the inability to see in low light (night blindness), which can lead to blindness if untreated.

Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, a main building block of strong bones, and protects against osteoporosis; the body makes it when bare skin is exposed to the sun (not through a window); fatty fish such as salmon, trout, tuna, and mackerel and fish liver oils are the best natural sources, with small amounts in beef liver, egg yolks, and cheese; deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in teens and adults.

Vitamin E is a fat-soluble nutrient that acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from damage caused by free radicals, and supports the immune system; the best sources are vegetable oils such as wheat germ, sunflower, and safflower oil, nuts such as almonds, sunflower seeds, and green vegetables like spinach and broccoli; deficiency is very rare in healthy people and usually tied to conditions in which fat is not properly digested or absorbed.

Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and healthy bones; green leafy vegetables such as spinach, kale, broccoli, and lettuce are major sources, along with vegetable oils, eggs, and some fruits, and bacteria in the colon make some vitamin K the body can absorb; severe deficiency causes bruising and bleeding problems because blood takes longer to clot.
Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed more easily by the body in the presence of dietary fat, so meals containing some fat help deliver vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Because fat-soluble vitamins are stored, the body keeps a reserve and they do not need to be eaten every single day; shortages of these vitamins tend to develop slowly rather than suddenly.

Excess is a real concern: high levels of vitamin D are almost always caused by excessive amounts from dietary supplements, and you cannot get too much vitamin D from sunshine because the skin limits production; high intakes of preformed vitamin A (usually from supplements) can cause severe headache, blurred vision, nausea, dizziness, muscle aches, and coordination problems and, in pregnancy, birth defects; high-dose vitamin E supplements might increase bleeding risk.

Food sources named in the lesson: liver, fish, dairy, and eggs (vitamin A); fatty fish, beef liver, egg yolks, and cheese (vitamin D); vegetable oils, nuts, and seeds (vitamin E); green leafy vegetables, vegetable oils, and eggs (vitamin K); and sunlight as the source the body uses to make vitamin D.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether sun exposure can cause vitamin D toxicity
positions: Popular worry that more sun means more vitamin D, and that sunbathing could cause an overdose

NIH ODS: the body makes vitamin D when bare skin is exposed to the sun, but the skin limits the amount it makes, so you cannot get too much vitamin D from sunshine; high blood levels are almost always caused by excessive supplement intake
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the ODS fact: sun exposure is self-limiting and is not a toxicity route; excess comes from concentrated supplement doses.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether all forms of vitamin A carry the same excess risk
positions: A single 'vitamin A toxicity' framing applied to all vitamin A sources

NIH ODS: high intakes of preformed vitamin A (from supplements or certain medicines) are the harmful ones, while high intakes of beta-carotene only turn skin yellow-orange and do not cause the same problems
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson distinguishes preformed vitamin A from provitamin A carotenoids when discussing toxicity, matching the ODS fact sheet.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How common fat-soluble vitamin deficiency actually is
positions: Deficiency conditions (night blindness, rickets, bleeding problems) sound alarming and are sometimes implied to be widespread

NIH ODS: vitamin A deficiency is rare in the United States but common in many developing countries; vitamin K deficiency is very rare; vitamin E deficiency is very rare in healthy people; vitamin D deficiency varies with sun exposure and other factors
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that deficiency is possible for each of the four but uncommon for most people eating varied diets, without dosing or scare content.

sourceRecords.title: Vitamin A and Carotenoids: Fact Sheet for Consumers
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamin A is fat-soluble and naturally present in many foods; roles in normal vision, immune system, reproduction, and growth; preformed vitamin A in fish, organ meats (liver), dairy, and eggs; provitamin A carotenoids (beta-carotene) in plant foods; deficiency sign xerophthalmia (inability to see in low light, can lead to blindness); high intakes of preformed vitamin A, usually from supplements, can cause severe headache, blurred vision, nausea, dizziness, muscle aches, and coordination problems and, in pregnancy, birth defects; high beta-carotene intake turns skin yellow-orange but lacks the same toxicity.

sourceRecords.title: Vitamin D: Fact Sheet for Consumers
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, a main building block for strong bones, and helps protect against osteoporosis; muscles and nerves need it; the body makes vitamin D when bare skin is exposed to the sun and does not make it through a window; fatty fish (trout, salmon, tuna, mackerel) and fish liver oils are the best natural sources, with small amounts in beef liver, egg yolks, and cheese; deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia (bone pain, muscle weakness) in teens and adults; high blood levels can cause nausea, vomiting, muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones, are almost always caused by excessive supplement intake, and the skin limits production so sun cannot cause excess.

sourceRecords.title: Vitamin E: Fact Sheet for Consumers
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamin E is a fat-soluble nutrient that acts as an antioxidant protecting cells from free-radical damage and boosts the immune system; best sources are vegetable oils (wheat germ, sunflower, safflower), corn and soybean oils, nuts (peanuts, hazelnuts, almonds), sunflower seeds, and green vegetables (spinach, broccoli); deficiency is very rare in healthy people and almost always linked to conditions in which fat is not properly digested or absorbed (Crohn's, cystic fibrosis); high supplement doses might increase the risk of bleeding and hemorrhagic stroke.

sourceRecords.title: Vitamin K: Fact Sheet for Consumers
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamin K is important for blood clotting and healthy bones; sources include green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale, broccoli, lettuce), vegetable oils, some fruits (blueberries, figs), meat, cheese, eggs, and soybeans; bacteria in the colon make some vitamin K the body can absorb; severe deficiency causes bruising and bleeding problems because blood takes longer to clot; deficiency is very rare in the United States.

sourceRecords.title: Vitamins (Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports the classification backbone: fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the body's liver, fatty tissue, and muscles; the four fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, and K; they are absorbed more easily by the body in the presence of dietary fat; water-soluble vitamins (C and the B vitamins) are not stored and excess leaves through urine — the contrast used in this lesson. Also used by the accepted vitamins sibling topic.
